power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Puberty is a period of major neural reorganization, accompanied by changing demands to navigate increasingly complex social environments and the emergence of many mental health disorders.
Although pubertal processes are becoming well-documented in neurotypical youth, the field has only begun to interrogate these processes in youth with autism.

In this mini-review, we evaluate evidence regarding altered pubertal development in autism based on studies examining physical development milestones and neuroendocrine axes pertinent to adrenarche and gonadarche.
We review studies linking pubertal factors with mental health symptoms in autistic youth to assess potential puberty-related links to risk for co-morbid psychopathology.
We bring together multiple literatures across human and animal models to assess evidence of consensus across fields.
Findings suggest that aspects of puberty may be accelerated in autism, and that they may be at elevated risk for co-morbid mental health symptoms.

We conclude with recommendations for future research, including the need for integration across pubertal, neural, and mental health measures to delineate how trajectories of risk may unfold in youth with autism.

Existing literature has demonstrated the profound influence of pubertal development on mental health in ostensibly neurotypical (NT) populations (Dehestani et al., 2023; Pfeifer & Allen, 2021), with evidence for marked increases in psychopathology symptoms in this adolescent developmental window (Blakemore, 2019).

text.text: Given that individuals with ASD may experience puberty in ways that diverge from their NT peers, it is crucial to examine how these changes impact their mental health, social interactions and relationships, cognition, as well as their overall well-being.

This conceptual mini-review aims to evaluate the extant literature on the neuroendocrine factors that contribute to pubertal development in individuals with ASD, shedding light on the unique challenges faced by this population during adolescence.

In what follows, we evaluate the current state of knowledge regarding various neuroendocrine axes and their development in ASD, including the hypothalamicpituitary-adrenal (HPA), hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG), and the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO [in females assigned at birth]) axes, and pubertal development patterns in youth with ASD.

To fully evaluate the existing body of evidence, this review bridges human and animal studies (where applicable) and the myriad of indices that characterize pubertal development (e.g., hormone levels, physical exams, questionnaires).

Given the known sensitive period that the adolescent window poses for the onset of most major mental health disorders (Solmi et al., 2022), we also weigh evidence for links between pubertal indices and co-morbid mental health issues in ASD.

text.text: We conclude with considerations and recommendations for future research to push the field forward toward designing studies to capture pubertal development and all its sequalae in autism.

text.text: The HPA axis regulates the body's homeostasis, responses to stress, and aspects of pubertal development (i.e., adrenarche).

Despite there being a longstanding literature on cortisol rhythms in ASD, there are mixed patterns regarding how and whether autistic individuals exhibit cortisol dysregulation compared to NT individuals.
Literature examining diurnal and acute cortisol responses in ASD has been systematically reviewed elsewhere (Taylor & Corbett, 2014; van der Linden et al., 2022).

text.text: Thus, we do not duplicate efforts here and instead focus our review on studies investigating the HPA-axis in the context of puberty and links made to symptomology in autistic youth (see Section 4.1).
In addition, we evaluate the extent to which animal models corroborate findings from human studies.

DHEA/DHEA-S. Adrenarche, the first major pubertal event, is spurred by rising production of androgens from the zona reticularis of the adrenal glands, including dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), its sulfate (DHEA-S) and androstenedione, under regulation of the HPA axis.
DHEA/DHEA-S levels begin to rise around 6-8 years of age (Rosenfield, 2021), with physical markers including pubic and axillary hair, as well as skin changes and body odor.

text.text: The HPG axis regulates the synthesis and release of sex steroid hormones, including testosterone and estradiol, across males and females.

Gonadarche, also referred to as central puberty, begins with the reactivation of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) signaling, which stimulates the production and major influx of sex steroid hormones involved in key physical and reproductive changes during puberty (e.g., growth spurts, facial hair growth, breast development, genital maturation, menarche).

A small but growing literature has examined whether autistic youth differ from neurotypical (NT) youth in circulating sex hormone levels, which may provide insight into differences in pubertal maturation and broader neuroendocrine functioning in ASD.
In what follows, we review literature on both testosterone and estrogen concentrations in youth with ASD (see Table 1 for overview).

text.text: Testosterone.
Studies examining differences in testosterone levels between those with ASD and NTs during development have largely yielded mixed results.

In early cross-sectional studies of testosterone levels collected from serum and saliva, youth with ASD had significantly lower testosterone levels than NT youth pre-and post-pubertal onset (Croonenberghs et al., 2010; Krajmer et al., 2011).

text.text: Similarly, recent longitudinal work has suggested that that boys with ASD may have blunted testosterone during adolescence compared to NTs (Corbett, McGonigle, et al., 2025; Sharpley et al., 2017).

text.text: In contrast, a few studies report elevated testosterone levels (via urine, and serum) in boys and girls with ASD compared to NT youth (Gasser et al., 2020; Hassan et al., 2019), as well as those with other psychiatric conditions (de Giambattista et al., 2025).

text.text: However, a number of studies also report no diagnostic differences in salivary or plasma testosterone levels in girls or boys cross-sectionally (Bakker-Huvenaars et al., 2020; Corbett, Calvosa, et al., 2025; Tordjman et al., 1995).

text.text: Findings appear to be indeterminate as to whether there are systematic differences in testosterone levels between those with and without ASD, and caution should be warranted when interpreting earlier studies, as they typically have much smaller samples and do not control for factors known to co-vary with testosterone concentrations (e.g., age, time of day).

Thus, future work would benefit from more rigorous investigation of how and whether testosterone levels may vary during gonadarche as a function of diagnosis, and whether this has any bearing on ASD symptom severity, neurodevelopment, and adaptive functioning.
Estrogen.
To date, very little work has focused on variability in estradiol levels during adolescence in autistic youth.
Estradiol is a key sex steroid hormone involved in gonadal maturation and pubertal development in both boys and girls and is also synthesized through the aromatization of testosterone.

Importantly, though it is often viewed as the primary sex hormone for females, estrogen does play a main regulatory role in physical changes in both boys and girls, including as an important driver of the pubertal growth spurt (Singh et al., 2010).

text.text: With respect to estradiol levels in ASD, multiple studies have reported no differences between autistic versus NT youth nor individuals with other psychiatric diagnoses (Al-Zaid et al., 2021; Corbett, Calvosa, et al., 2025; de Giambattista et al., 2025).

text.text: Similar to testosterone, initial investigations of estradiol levels during adolescence remain largely inconclusive, with most studies reporting no group differences.

However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, as this literature is primarily crosssectional and often limited by methodological concerns related to sample size and hormone modeling approaches (e.g., covariate selection and treatment of hormone data).

Future work would benefit from larger, prospectively followed cohorts that are carefully characterized with respect to pubertal maturation in order to better capture developmental changes in hormone dynamics across adolescence and determine whether estradiol trajectories systematically differ in ASD.
Importantly, inconsistent findings in circulating estradiol concentrations in ASD do not necessarily exclude a role for estrogen signaling in ASD neurobiology.

Experimental studies have demonstrated that postnatal administration of 17β-estradiol to Pvalb heterozygous mice increased parvalbumin expression within cortical interneurons and significantly improved deficits in social interaction and repetitive behaviors (Filice et al., 2018).

text.text: These findings suggest that altered tissue responsiveness to sex steroids, rather than differences in circulating hormone concentrations alone, may contribute to neurodevelopmental phenotypes and highlight the importance of considering both endocrine and cellspecific mechanisms when investigating gonadal steroid signaling in ASD.
Animal Models.
Compared with extensive behavioral, synaptic, and circuit-level characterization, reproductive neuroendocrine phenotyping has received relatively little attention in rodent models of ASD.
Among existing models, Mecp2 deletion-associated with Rett Syndrome-has undergone the most comprehensive endocrine characterization.

A recent study of Rett syndrome mice demonstrated delayed pubertal maturation accompanied by reduced circulating testosterone, decreased luteinizing hormone (LH), and impaired GnRH signaling despite preservation of GnRH neuron number (Martín-Sánchez et al., 2026), suggesting that MECP2 deficiency disrupts functional maturation of hypothalamic reproductive circuits rather than their developmental specification.

text.text: Consistent with this interpretation, androgenresponsive vasopressin circuitry was similarly reduced, indicating that altered testosterone signaling extends beyond reproductive tissues to influence sexually dimorphic neural networks.

Conversely, mouse models of MECP2 duplication syndrome exhibit elevated circulating testosterone with relatively preserved estradiol concentrations (Wang et al., 2021), demonstrating that both increased and decreased MECP2 dosage disrupt androgen homeostasis through distinct, likely epigenetically mediated mechanisms.

text.text: Evidence for HPG axis dysfunction has also emerged from Fmr1 mouse models of Fragile X syndrome, although the literature is less integrated.

Independent studies have reported alterations in testosterone, estradiol, gonadotropin secretion, gonadal maturation, and fertility, consistent with impaired reproductive endocrine regulation (Elmazoudy et al., 2026).

text.text: However, these investigations have largely arisen from studies of reproductive physiology rather than neurodevelopment, and relatively few have examined hypothalamic GnRH circuitry or pubertal progression alongside behavioral phenotypes.

Together, animal studies suggest that disruption of genes implicated in neurodevelopment can influence pubertal maturation and reproductive endocrine function, supporting the concept that altered HPG axis development may represent an intrinsic component of at least a subset of ASD.
At the same time, they highlight substantial gaps in the field which are largely echoed among the human literature.

text.text: In what follows, we review two separate but interrelated lines of research here, including general trends of pubertal timing, stage, tempo, and patterns of precocious puberty in autism.

In studies of pubertal timing, there has been some evidence for earlier onset of puberty in adolescents with ASD compared to NT peers (Corbett et al., 2020 (Corbett et al., , 2022;; Groenman et al., 2024) with mixed results regarding age at menarche for girls.

No within-sex diagnostic group-level differences in adrenarcheal processes (i.e., pubic hair development) were observed.

Another recent study revealed that girls with and without autism did not differ in age of menarche, but that overall, youth with ASD started gonadarche, but not adrenarche, earlier than TD youth (Groenman et al., 2024).

Given the longitudinal nature of this study, they also examined the tempo or pace of pubertal development.
However, no differences were found between youth with and without autism for either gonadarche or adrenarche tempo.
Similar to the cross-sectional Corbett et al., 2020 study, girls with ASD started gonadarche earlier than NT girls but did not show any timing differences for adrenarche.
There were also no significant diagnostic differences for boys in their timing and tempo of gonadarche or adrenarche.

Conversely, with an additional year of data (i.e., 4 time points), Corbett and colleagues report no differences in breast development timing and tempo between ASD and NT girls, though other physical markers of puberty were not examined for timing and tempo differences (Corbett, Calvosa, et al., 2025).

Another key difference between these studies is how pubertal development was assessed.
The Corbett studies used the gold-standard method of having a physician assess pubertal stage, whereas the Groenman study used the self-report Pubertal Development Scale (Carskadon & Acebo, 1993).

A few studies have examined precocious puberty (PP) in autism, which is defined as the onset of gonadarche or secondary-sex characteristics (e.g., breast development, menses in girls, and genital development) by age 8 in girls and 9 in boys (Sharma & Daley, 2026).

text.text: This is distinguishable from earlier pubertal timing within the normal range, as PP is a diagnosable condition and may indicate more significant dysfunction in endocrine systems.

However, it should be noted that most studies to date that have examined general pubertal patterns have not systematically evaluated their samples for a PP diagnosis, which does not rule out the possibility that some autistic children in those samples had undiagnosed PP.

That said, the notion that PP is generally overrepresented in ASD is a crucial insight into potential alterations in patterns of endocrine development and how they differ in ASD compared to the NT population.
Existing studies have used a range of methods, from case-based (Finkle et al., 2020) to epidemiological methods, to establish whether PP is disproportionate in autism (see Table 2).

text.text: As an example, Tsai et al. (2024) utilized data from 11,104 children with ASD and age-, sex-matched NT children (85.8% male; N=22,208) based upon PP diagnoses made by medical professionals (e.g., pediatricians, endocrinologists).

text.text: Crucially, autistic girls were at an even greater risk of developing PP during the follow-up period than autistic boys (girls = 3.5%, boys= 0.3%).

Although the rate of risk differs, two separate epidemiological samples have shown significantly increased risk of PP in autism compared to children without autism, ranging from a 1.94-fold increase to a 4-fold increase in risk for PP (Geier & Geier, 2021; Hueg et al., 2026).

text.text: Taken together, this small collection of studies suggests that autistic youth, and autistic girls in particular, are at an elevated risk of undergoing PP than their non-autistic counterparts.

This provides additional support for the idea that there may be systematic alterations or even subtypes of ASD that are characterized by altered neuroendocrine axis functioning that results in earlier onset of secondary-sex characteristic development.
What is less clear in this literature is whether these patterns are due to central or peripheral PP.
Central PP is thought to be due to earlier triggering of gonadarche or HPG axis activity (e.g., earlier increases in GnRH).

At the same time, peripheral PP is due to an influx of sex steroid hormones instigated by processes independent of premature hypothalamus/pituitary activity (e.g., elevated sex steroid hormone production in gonads or adrenal glands).
Moreover, the extent to which there are differential consequences for neural and behavioral development in individuals with ASD versus NTs to either central or peripheral PP is unexplored.

Thus, future work should consider making more targeted attempts to disentangle sources of PP in autism and their associations with children's mental and physical health, given the known links between pubertal development and emergent mental health problems in the general population (Dehestani et al., 2023).

text.text: Given this prominent risk and the known risk for mental health symptom onset and progression during puberty more broadly (Kretzer et al., 2024; Pfeifer & Allen, 2021), we briefly review the emerging literature documenting whether variability in pubertal factors influence mental health functioning in ASD (Table 2).

text.text: In what follows, we combine our review of mental health links to physical markers of puberty and pubertal hormones, as the literature is limited across methods of pubertal assessment.
In terms of physical markers of puberty, there is a small collection of studies examining potential links between pubertal status and mental health functioning in youth with ASD.
Cross-sectionally, one study has shown that earlier gonadal and adrenal timing are related to more depressive and externalizing symptoms in youth with ASD (Groenman et al., 2024).

text.text: Conversely, in a 4-year longitudinal study across ages 10-16 years old, otherwise NT youth showed increasing depressive symptoms with age and advancing gonadal development, while youth with ASD showed decreasing symptoms with age and puberty (Corbett et al., 2024).

text.text: In fact, ASD had higher depressive symptoms earlier in pubertal development.

In the same cohort, Corbett and colleagues report that adrenarche and gonadarche timing were not associated with internalizing symptoms (i.e., anxiety, affective problems) in boys or girls with ASD (Corbett et al., 2022).

text.text: Another longitudinal study of 11-17 year-olds suggests that boys with late pubertal onset, irrespective of ASD diagnostic status, had increasing emotional and peer problems across 3 time points, and girls showed no effects of pubertal timing on changes in symptoms (Dawe-Lane et al., 2025).

text.text: In terms of pubertal hormones, multiple studies examining links between testosterone levels in boys and girls with ASD report no associations with social symptoms as a function of diagnosis (Corbett, McGonigle, et al., 2025; Muscatello et al., 2022).

text.text: Altogether, this scant, mixed literature underscores the need for more studies, especially with longitudinal designs, to continue to parse trajectories of mental health symptoms in youth with ASD, as they may continue to change in the transition from adolescence to emerging adulthood when social dynamics increase in complexity and access to mental health and support services decreases.

Indeed, longitudinal population-based work has shown that during adolescence, those with ASD and autistic traits exhibit increasing depressive symptoms from 10 to 18 years old, and that bullying amplifies this risk (Rai et al., 2018).

text.text: One potential explanation for the previously reviewed mixed findings is that puberty may not exert uniform effects on mental health in ASD, but instead interact with developmental timing, social context, sex, and pre-existing symptom profiles to shape heterogeneous trajectories across adolescence.

Collectively, these findings suggest that adolescence likely represents a period of elevated vulnerability for co-morbid mental health conditions in ASD, though the findings reviewed here remain inconclusive with respect to the role of puberty pe se.
Future work should also consider a broader constellation of symptoms beyond internalizing and externalizing behaviors.

For instance, nearly 88% of autistic individuals in a sample of 7-70 year olds reported experiencing suicidal thoughts, with about a third attempting suicide in their lifetime (Schwartzman et al., 2025), underscoring the substantial psychiatric burden experienced by many autistic individuals.

text.text: However, it remains unclear how suicidality may relate to pubertal development specifically.
Moreover, it may be the case that puberty alone does not fully capture milestones pertinent to autistic youths' mental health and adaptive functioning.

For instance, the transition into middle school may be especially disruptive for autistic youths' mental health functioning in ways that differ from NT youth, as highlighted in prior qualitative work (Makin et al., 2017; Nuske et al., 2019).

text.text: Although emerging work suggests that pubertal development may relate to mental health trajectories in autistic youth, the biological and psychological mechanisms underlying these associations remain poorly characterized.

In particular, it remains unclear whether variability in pubertal maturation and hormone dynamics in ASD reflects alterations in central neuroendocrine regulation, peripheral gonadal or adrenal processes, and/or broader interactions between neuroendocrine function and the social demands of adolescence.
Greater mechanistic specificity will be critical for understanding how pubertal processes may contribute to heterogeneity in co-morbid mental health outcomes that are frequently reported in ASD.

In what follows, we provide several concrete recommendations for future research seeking to clarify these developmental pathways in the hopes of spurring new research directions (see Figure 1 for a conceptual overview).

We propose that the confluence of pubertal processes and the major reorganization of neural circuitry serving social affective and higher-order cognitive processing during adolescence in concert with increasingly complex social dynamics likely all work in concert to put youth with autism at increased risk for a range of mental health symptoms.
In the two boxes, we briefly outline current evidence relating these factors in autism, as well as gaps in the literature and potential future directions identified through this mini-review.
Despite existing work providing foundational insights, several methodological improvements should be at the fore of studies characterizing pubertal development in autism.

Specifically, much of the earlier work in this area has consisted of small samples that, in some cases, were not appropriately matched on age, which can limit interpretability of puberty-related effects that are frequently confounded by age.

Moreover, smaller samples reporting null effects (e.g., in the pubertal hormone literature) have made it difficult to discern whether the lack of effects is due to power and design issues, or actual phenomenon.

It is also unclear how well the current literature captures the full spectrum, and whether extant samples are enriched for specific presentations of autism (e.g., more or less severe syndromic samples).

Thus, greater investment in expressly designing well-powered studies with well-characterized samples examining pubertal development in autism are sorely needed to advance our understanding of these processes.

In addition, current research on pubertal development in ASD is largely cross-sectional, with only one ongoing longitudinal study specifically designed to rigorously track these developmental changes (Corbett, Calvosa, et al., 2025; Corbett et al., 2022 Corbett et al., , 2024;; Corbett, McGonigle, et al., 2025).

text.text: While studies have explored specific pubertal and neuroendocrine processes in autism, such as precocious puberty (Tsai et al., 2024), menarche/menstruation (Skommer & Gunesh, 2025), and variability in hormones (Bakker-Huvenaars et al., 2020), there remains a significant gap capturing how these dynamic and nonlinear processes fluctuate over time.

text.text: Future research should prioritize comprehensive longitudinal designs that track pubertal onset, progression, and the concurrent changes in mental health across adolescence in individuals with ASD.

Such studies are essential for clarifying critical periods of vulnerability or resilience, establishing more causal links between pubertal processes and mental health trajectories, and ultimately informing timely and targeted interventions.
There also continue to be open questions regarding how to accurately assess pubertal development in individuals with ASD.

Evidence suggests that parents of children with ASD tend to be less accurate and underestimate their child's pubertal stage compared to parents of NT youth, though there has been acceptable agreement reported with gold standard physical exam staging (Corbett et al., 2019).

text.text: Notably, boys and girls with and without ASD had largely comparable levels of concordance between physical exams and their self-reported pubertal status, ranging from poor to fair.

Although self-report measures tend to be less concordant with physical exams, they may offer important insight into how autistic adolescents perceive and interpret their bodily changes, and these perceptions may have greater relevance for mental health functioning than objective pubertal indices.

Indeed, work in otherwise NT adolescents suggests that perceived pubertal timing and physically observable pubertal maturation tend to show more consistent associations with transdiagnostic mental health symptoms than hormonal measures alone (Barendse et al., 2022; Dehestani et al., 2024), potentially because adolescents' perceptions of their bodily changes may shape social experiences, self-image, peer relationships, and feelings of social difference during adolescence.

text.text: This may be particularly relevant and uniquely challenging for autistic youth, as adolescence involves increasingly complex social milieu that occur alongside substantial physical and developmental changes.

Ultimately, studies examining pubertal development in autistic youth should opt to take a comprehensive, multi-method approach whenever possible, incorporating parent and self-report measures alongside hormonal assessments.
Ultimately, characterizing how pubertal processes contribute to mental health trajectories in autistic youth will require the integration of neurodevelopmental and pubertal measures.

Pubertal hormones instigate enormous changes in the brain and social-affective behaviors during adolescence (Pfeifer & Allen, 2021; Sisk & Foster, 2004), and although there is an extensive literature examining neurodevelopment in autistic adolescents (Durkut et al., 2022; Rafiee et al., 2022; Uddin et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2025), studies have not explicitly linked these processes to concurrent pubertal maturation.

text.text: Crucially, puberty captures biological variability in adolescent development that is not fully reflected by chronological age alone, potentially offering additional explanatory insight into heterogeneity in neurodevelopmental and mental health trajectories in ASD.
In other words, integrating neuroimaging with hormonal and pubertal assessments could help address several outstanding questions in autism research that age-related development alone cannot capture.

For instance, puberty may differentially shape the maturation of the sensorimotor-association axis in ASD versus NT youth, particularly given that higher-order association regions continue to undergo prolonged remodeling throughout adolescence, are enriched with sex hormone receptors, and support complex behaviors that are affected in autism (e.g., social-affective processing).

Likewise, emerging work on menstrual cycle-related brain dynamics (Heller et al., 2025) raises important questions regarding how cyclical hormonal fluctuations affect brain function and mental health in autistic girls, who may be at elevated risk for more severe menstrual symptoms, irregular menses, and menstrual disorders (Skommer & Gunesh, 2025).

text.text: Neuroimaging approaches may also provide insight into how pubertal indices influence excitatory/inhibitory balance in ASD, for example by leveraging magnetic resonance spectroscopy to examine neurochemical profiles in hormone-sensitive brain regions.

Finally, emerging neuroimaging technologies such as optically-pumped magnetometer MEG (OPM-MEG), which enables wearable, motion-tolerant recording, and interpersonal hyperscanning (e.g., scanning dyads simultaneously), stands to provide novel opportunities to examine how autistic youth interact with peers and caregivers in real time and how these social neural dynamics change as a function of pubertal development.

Collectively, integrating brain-based and neuroendocrine approaches will be critical for disentangling the interacting biological mechanisms that shape adolescent development and mental health risk in autism.

Further elucidating these biological mechanisms will also benefit from greater attention to interactions across neuroendocrine systems during puberty, particularly potential cross-axis coupling or decoupling between the HPA and HPG axes in autistic youth.
If autism is characterized by differences in neuroendocrine dynamics, it will be important for different endocrine axes to be considered in tandem, rather than in isolation.

Existing work suggests that there are potential alterations to HPA-axis functioning in ASD (Taylor & Corbett, 2014), primarily based on diurnal cortisol rhythms and acute responses to stressors, though findings are mixed.

text.text: Although patterns are mixed, and likely context dependent, with respect to hypo-versus hyper-responsiveness of the HPA-axis in autism, altered coordination between stress-related and gonadal hormone systems may be one pathway through which pubertal development contributes to heterogeneity in mental health and developmental outcomes.

Moreover, more attention to the component parts of neuroendocrine axes, including the hypothalamus and pituitary gland, will be necessary for capturing where within the feedback loops central to pubertal hormone regulation alterations may arise in autism.
For instance, in otherwise NT youth, critical links between pubertal indices, pituitary gland volume, and mental health symptoms have been documented (Murray et al., 2016; Picci et al., 2025).

text.text: Complementing human studies, cross-species research utilizing animal models can provide invaluable insights into these complex biological interactions.
Given the ethical and practical limitations of hormonal manipulation studies in humans, future research should leverage animal models to gain a deeper understanding of pubertal development in ASD.

This should include comprehensive and prospective research design to probe pubertal development rather than retrospective secondary data analysis (e.g., observed timing of vaginal opening or first pregnancy as part of an unrelated study).
Animal models offer controlled environments to investigate the direct impact of hormonal changes on neurodevelopmental processes and behavior relevant to ASD.

Insights from animal studies can then inform observational research in humans, helping to identify potential biomarkers, refine hypotheses, and uncover novel therapeutic targets that are not feasible to explore through human studies alone.
However, current popular model systems may not be sufficient, particularly for the study of adrenarche.

Indeed, the spiny mouse, which does experience a natural rise in DHEA ahead of reproductive maturation (Quinn et al., 2016), has been used as an orphan model system for reproductive endocrinology for decades.

text.text: This model may prove particularly powerful for studying the intersection between pubertal development and ASD but will require time and effort to generate the necessary genetic tools for doing so.
Most major mental health disorders emerge during adolescence, with 50% onsetting by age 14 and 75% by age 25 (Solmi et al., 2022).

text.text: This period of heightened psychiatric vulnerability, coupled with the substantial neural reorganization that occurs during puberty, underscores the importance of clarifying how pubertal processes may shape mental health risk in autistic youth.

Although co-morbid mental health concerns during adolescence have long been documented in ASD (Anderson et al., 2011; Billstedt et al., 2005; Mayes et al., 2011), existing work linking puberty to mental health has largely focused on internalizing symptoms or exacerbation of core autism-related features (Corbett et al., 2024).

text.text: Future research should broaden this scope to include other symptom domains and transdiagnostic processes that autistic youth are at elevated risk for.

For example, suicidal ideation and self-injurious thoughts and behaviors increase markedly during adolescence in otherwise NT populations, and autistic individuals show substantially elevated rates of suicidality relative to NT peers across development and adulthood (Schwartzman et al., 2025).

text.text: However, despite this heightened risk, virtually nothing is known about how pubertal timing, tempo, or hormone dynamics may contribute to suicidality risk in autistic youth specifically.

More broadly, future work should examine how pubertal factors relate to the exacerbation or mitigation of diverse psychiatric and transdiagnostic symptoms across adolescence, and whether these developmental trajectories diverge from NT peers.
Another critical area for future research is understanding how pubertal and neurodevelopmental processes shape the transition into adult social roles for autistic individuals.

This developmental transition may pose unique challenges for autistic youth, who are often at elevated risk for difficulties related to independent living, employment, higher education, and social integration in adulthood (Esbensen et al., 2010; Matson et al., 2009; Neely & Hunter, 2014; Solomon, 2020).

text.text: Existing work suggests that autistic youth exhibit distinct trajectories of brain development relative to NT peers in domains supporting the successful transition into adult social roles (Picci & Scherf, 2015), raising the possibility that pubertal processes may interact with (or in some cases, provoke) atypical neurodevelopmental processes to influence such vulnerable domains and, by extension, mental health outcomes during this crucial developmental transition.

text.text: Given that this developmental period coincides with the peak emergence of major psychiatric disorders, future longitudinal work should clarify how pubertal maturation and neurodevelopment jointly contribute to resilience versus vulnerability as autistic youth move into adulthood.

Understanding these interacting developmental pathways will be critical for generating developmentally-informed supports and targeted interventions that are tailored to facilitate autistic individuals' long-term mental health and adaptive outcomes.

text.text: Alongside mental health measures (KSADS, CBCL), the ABCD dataset provides a valuable resource for charting developmental trajectories in a large representative sample.
Although autism is not the focus of ABCD, Social Responsiveness Scale data are available, which can in principle be used to measure autistic traits.
Future work may utilize this large longitudinal dataset to explore links between puberty, mental health, and autism symptoms.

Emerging evidence suggests that pubertal development may unfold differently in autism, with the most consistent findings pointing to differences in pubertal timing (i.e., primarily gonadarche) and increased risk for precocious puberty, particularly among autistic girls.

However, findings regarding pubertal hormone concentrations and their associations with mental health remain mixed, highlighting substantial heterogeneity within autism as well as methodological limitations of the existing literature.
Critically, puberty is a complex neuroendocrine process that cannot be adequately characterized by agerelated changes, circulating hormone concentrations, or physical maturation alone.

We propose that progress in this area will require prospective, longitudinal studies like ABCD that are designed specifically to capture pubertal development in autism, with sufficiently powered and well-characterized samples and multimethod assessment of neuroendocrine, physical, neural, and psychological changes.

Complementary cross-species work will also be vital for identifying mechanisms linking pubertal neuroendocrine changes to brain and behavioral development that cannot be readily or ethically isolated in humans, particularly when pubertal development is prospectively characterized rather than captured incidentally in existing animal models.

Together, these approaches will be essential for determining whether and how pubertal processes contribute to divergent neurodevelopmental and mental health trajectories in autistic youth and for identifying developmental windows in which targeted supports may be most beneficial.
